items.prompt: Explain why a business needs its employees to be motivated if it is to meet its objectives.
items.canonical_answer: Because labour is the one input whose output depends on willingness. A machine hired for eight hours delivers eight hours of capacity; an employee paid for eight hours delivers somewhere between the least that avoids trouble and the most they are capable of, and motivation decides where in that range they work. The purpose of raising it is what happens in the channels that follow: output per employee, days lost to unplanned absence, the proportion of staff leaving and needing replacement, reject and complaint rates, and the improvement ideas employees bring forward. Those are the figures through which effort reaches survival, profit or a service target.
marking_guidance: Reason: labour is the input whose output varies with willingness, which is why it can be managed at all.
Purpose: the answer must say why the business needs this, reaching at least one named business objective.
Reward at least one named channel - productivity, absence, turnover, quality or ideas - rather than a jump straight to profit.

items.prompt: Analyse how a fall in labour turnover among skilled staff can reduce a manufacturer's costs.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is a workforce whose skills take months to build. Where motivation rises and fewer skilled employees leave, the business advertises and selects less often, so recruitment spending falls. It also runs fewer induction and training programmes, so the direct cost of preparing replacements falls. The mechanism that usually matters most is the third: a new employee works below the output and above the reject rate of an experienced one for the first weeks, so every post that does not turn over avoids that period of lost output and wasted material. The measurable consequence is a lower cost of output per unit produced, which widens the gap between price and cost and supports a profit objective. The chain holds where the skills genuinely take time to acquire; in work that a new starter can do at full speed within a day, the third mechanism contributes little and only the recruitment spending is saved.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain depends on the skills taking time to acquire, and that condition must be stated.
Mechanism: recruitment spending, training cost and the output lost while a replacement learns.
Consequence: a measurable effect on cost per unit, not simply 'costs fall'.
The business objective reached must be named.

items.prompt: A contact centre in Windhoek employs 40 agents, works 22 days a month and loses 9% of scheduled days to unplanned absence. It buys cover from an agency at N$950 a day. Explain how cutting absence to 5% would affect its costs.
items.canonical_answer: Scheduled days are 40 x 22 = 880 a month. At 9%, days lost are 880 x 0.09 = 79.2, and the agency bill is 79.2 x N$950 = N$75 240 a month. At 5%, days lost are 880 x 0.05 = 44 and the bill is 44 x N$950 = N$41 800. The centre saves N$33 440 a month. The reason the saving is this large is specific to this business: it covers absence with bought-in agency staff at a day rate, so absence converts directly into an invoice rather than being absorbed by colleagues.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the centre's own facts - 40 agents, 22 days, the 9% rate and the N$950 day rate.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that absence is covered by bought-in agency days, so it has a price attached.
Conclusion: a figure for the saving must be reached, in N$.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to treat a satisfied workforce as the same thing as a motivated one?
items.canonical_answer: Because satisfaction measures how employees feel about their situation and motivation measures the effort they are willing to give, and the two can move apart. An employee may be contented precisely because the job asks little of them, and another may be dissatisfied with their pay while still working hard at a task they care about. A business that surveys how happy its staff say they are has therefore measured something other than effort, and should read the output, absence and quality figures alongside it.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must say why the belief is wrong, not only that it is.
Reward the point that contentment can come from a job that asks little.

items.prompt: Explain one reason why raising motivation may not raise a business's output.
items.canonical_answer: Because willingness raises output only where the employee also has the skill, the equipment, the materials and the authority to act on it. A motivated machinist whose machine keeps breaking down produces nothing extra, and a motivated clerk who must refer every decision upwards still works at the speed of the person above. Motivation is one determinant of productivity among several, so where the binding constraint is maintenance, training or the right to decide, a business can raise willingness and see the output figure barely move.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed to a consequence, so that it says what the business would observe.
Reward the point that motivation is one determinant among several, with the binding constraint named.

items.prompt: Define a human need.

items.prompt: Explain why a reward that changed an employee's behaviour two years ago may do very little today.
items.canonical_answer: Because a need that has been largely met tends to lose its power to direct behaviour, and another need moves into its place as the one pressing hardest. Nothing about the reward has changed; what has changed is that the need it answered is no longer urgent for that person. An employee for whom a wage increase once decided whether the rent was paid may now have that need settled, so the same increase is received as pleasant rather than as a reason to work differently, while a need the wage does not touch - recognition, or work that stretches them - has moved to the front.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must say why, resting on a satisfied need losing its power to direct behaviour.
Purpose: the answer must explain the consequence for an employer choosing rewards.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a need and a want, and why the difference matters to an employer.
items.canonical_answer: A need is a requirement a person acts to satisfy; a want is a preference about how to satisfy it. The boundary matters because an employer can rarely give people the particular thing they ask for, but can often answer the need underneath it by another route. Two employees may share the same need for security and want quite different things - one a permanent contract, the other a medical aid scheme for a sick relative. An employer who hears only the want sees two unrelated demands; one who hears the need sees a single problem with more than one possible answer.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: the requirement itself against the preferred way of meeting it, with the consequence for the employer stated.

items.prompt: Explain how an unmet need affects the way an employee behaves at work.
items.canonical_answer: An unmet need creates a tension, and the person acts to remove it, so their attention and effort are pulled towards whatever would meet it. The stronger the need, the more of that attention it takes. An employee who cannot cover their household costs attends to overtime, to a second job or to a better-paid vacancy elsewhere; an employee with no company at work attends to the few chances there are to talk. The behaviour an employer observes - absence, a resignation, a request for a transfer, effort concentrated on one part of the job - is that person acting on the need that presses hardest.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must show how the need produces the behaviour, not only that it does.
Because the tension is what drives action, the answer must connect need to observable behaviour at work.

items.prompt: Explain how work satisfies human needs by two different routes.
items.canonical_answer: Indirectly, through pay: the money itself meets nothing, but it buys food, housing, transport and school fees, and it can be saved against future trouble, so everything pay does for a person's needs it does outside the workplace. Directly, through the job: the company of colleagues, the standing a role carries, the interest of the work and the sense of having done something well are received at work and cannot be bought elsewhere with the same wage. Keeping the two routes apart is how a business sees that raising the wage cannot answer a need that is only ever met inside the job.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: both routes must be explained, showing how each reaches the need.
Because pay acts outside the workplace and the job acts inside it, the answer must reach the consequence for an employer.

items.prompt: A lodge outside Swakopmund employs 30 staff on identical terms: N$7 200 a month, shared accommodation and one meal a shift. Petrus is 19, lives with his family in town and is saving for a college course; Selma is 41 and the only earner for four dependants. Explain why the same offer of paid training is likely to affect them differently.
items.canonical_answer: Because the two arrive with different needs pressing hardest, even though the terms are identical. For Petrus the household is not depending on his wage and the course he is saving for shows what he is reaching for, so training answers the need to grow and improves his prospects - it is aimed at the need he actually has. For Selma the binding constraint is a household budget supported by one income and the risk of the job ending; training is pleasant but secondary, and what would change her behaviour is a permanent contract, medical aid or hours she can rely on. The same offer therefore reaches one of them and largely passes the other by.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the lodge's own facts - identical terms, Petrus's savings goal, Selma's four dependants.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the need pressing hardest differs, so the same reward has different value.
Conclusion: the answer must reach a clear statement of which employee the offer reaches and what would reach the other.

items.prompt: Explain one way in which a job may fail to satisfy an employee's need for security.
items.canonical_answer: By offering work on short or casual contracts renewed at short notice. items.prompt: Analyse how employing production staff on repeated short casual contracts can affect the quality of their work.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is a workforce whose contracts are renewed at short notice, so the need for security is unmet. Because an unmet need pulls attention towards whatever would meet it, employees in this position give part of their attention to finding more permanent work, and the ones who succeed leave. The mechanism that reaches quality is what follows: the business is repeatedly working with people in their first weeks on the job, who are still learning the standard and the method, and it has less reason to invest in training people it may not keep. The measurable consequence is a higher reject or rework rate and more customer complaints, which raises the cost of output and can damage the business's reputation with its buyers. The chain runs strongest where the work takes time to learn; where a new starter reaches the standard within a day, the effect on quality is much smaller and only the loss of continuity remains.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain starts from insecure contracts leaving the security need unmet, and its strength depends on how long the work takes to learn.
Mechanism: attention diverted, departures, and a workforce repeatedly in its first weeks.
Consequence: a measurable effect on reject or rework rates and complaints.
The effect on the business - cost of output and reputation with buyers - must be reached.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a content theory of motivation and a process theory.
items.canonical_answer: They answer different questions. A content theory asks what motivates people - which needs or rewards make effort worthwhile - and Taylor, Mayo, Maslow, Herzberg and McClelland are all content theories. A process theory asks how motivation comes about, meaning the thinking that turns a reward on offer into effort actually given, and Vroom's expectancy theory is the process theory named in this syllabus. The consequence of the boundary is practical: a content theory tells a business what to put on the table, while a process theory tells it whether what it has put there will be picked up.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, each with at least one named theorist.
Boundary: what motivates against how motivation arises, and the consequence for a business must be stated.

items.prompt: A business has raised pay twice in two years and seen no change in output per employee. Analyse why the motivation theories would send it to look somewhere other than pay.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is that pay has already been raised twice, so whatever need money answers for these employees is now largely answered. On Herzberg's account pay is a hygiene factor: correcting it removes a reason for dissatisfaction without by itself producing positive effort, so a third increase acts on a scale that is already at neutral. Taylor's prescription would be to tie the pay to measured output rather than to raise it flat, which this business has not done, so even the theory most favourable to money predicts little from what it did. The mechanism running through both is that effort responds to the need that is still unmet, and further money reaches a need that is not. The measurable consequence is exactly what the business observed: a higher wage bill with output per employee unchanged, so its cost per unit has risen. The reasoning holds where pay was already adequate; where employees are paid below what a household needs, money behaves quite differently and the diagnosis would be wrong.
marking_guidance: Condition: the reasoning depends on pay already being adequate, and that condition must be stated.
Mechanism: effort responds to the need still unmet, so further money acts where the need is already answered.
Consequence: the answer must reach a measurable result - wage bill up, output per employee unchanged, cost per unit higher.
The effect on the business or on a named objective must be reached.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a business should pick one motivation theory and apply it consistently across its whole workforce.
items.canonical_answer: It should not. The decisive criterion is that the theories answer different questions about different needs, so choosing one means leaving the others' questions unasked, and a workforce rarely has a single unmet need. In a business with production staff on shift rates and professional staff on salaries, the diagnosis at the two ends is unlikely to be the same, and a single theory applied across both will fit one and misfit the other. The strongest argument for a single theory is consistency: one framework is easier for managers to learn, easier to apply fairly, and less open to the charge that different groups are treated differently - which is a real objection, because perceived unfairness in reward is itself demotivating. The better course is to keep the diagnosis separate from the framework: use Herzberg to check that pay and conditions are not causing dissatisfaction, Maslow or McClelland to identify what is unmet for a particular group, and Vroom to test whether the reward chosen will actually be chased. The judgement would change in a very small business with one kind of work and a handful of employees, where one framework may genuinely cover everyone and the cost of running several is not worth paying.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the recommendation must be argued for a workforce doing different kinds of work.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that the theories answer different questions about different unmet needs.
Counterargument: must address the case for consistency and the demotivating effect of perceived unfairness.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement - a very small business with one kind of work.

items.prompt: A Namibian retailer offers its branch assistants a N$2 000 monthly bonus for the best-performing branch. Take-up of the scheme is enthusiastic in three branches and ignored in the other nine. Explain which question Vroom's theory answers here that Maslow's does not.
items.canonical_answer: Maslow's hierarchy answers what the assistants need, and it would say the same thing in all twelve branches: on identical pay and conditions, the level reached is broadly similar, so the theory cannot explain why the response differs. Vroom's theory answers whether a particular reward will be chased, which is the question the retailer actually has. In this case the three enthusiastic branches are presumably ones whose assistants believe they can win - expectancy is high - while assistants in nine branches that have never come close believe their effort cannot produce the required performance, so expectancy is near zero and the whole force of the scheme collapses whatever the money is worth. The retailer's problem is therefore in the design of the target rather than in the size of the bonus.

items.prompt: Identify, in order, the steps Taylor's scientific management prescribes for a repetitive manual task.
items.canonical_answer: Begin from what you have: the task as it is currently done, and the ability to observe and time it. First, observe and time the existing method. Second, break the task into its simple repeated elements and identify the quickest sound way to carry out each. Third, calculate a standard output from the timings. Fourth, select employees suited to the task and train every one of them to the single method. Fifth, set a piece rate that rewards output above the standard. Sixth, supervise closely to see the method is followed. What you finish with is a defined method, a standard output and a pay rule that moves with the number of units produced.
marking_guidance: Steps must be given in order, beginning with observing and timing the existing method.

Each step must state the action taken - observe, break down, calculate, select, train, set the rate, supervise.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of Taylor's approach in a service business such as a private clinic.
items.canonical_answer: The approach depends on output that can be counted and checked, and much of what a clinic's staff do cannot be. Patients seen per hour is countable, but it is a poor measure of the work, because the care given to a difficult case is exactly what a count ignores. The developed consequence is that tying pay to the countable measure would push staff towards shorter consultations, so the clinic would raise the figure it was paying for and lower the quality it depends on for its reputation.

items.prompt: Analyse how paying a piece rate, as Taylor recommended, can raise output and damage quality at the same time.

The business meets this by adding inspection, which costs money and offsets part of the gain, so the net effect on profit depends on whether the extra output is worth more than the extra inspection and scrap. items.prompt: Evaluate the usefulness of Maslow's hierarchy to a manager deciding how to motivate 200 production employees.
items.canonical_answer: It is useful as a way of framing the question and unreliable as a way of answering it, and a manager should use it only alongside evidence from the workforce itself. The decisive criterion is that the hierarchy offers no way of telling which level a particular employee has reached, so with 200 employees the manager is applying a judgement to a group that almost certainly contains several different answers - some supporting households on the wage, others long settled and bored. Acting on a single diagnosis across all of them risks spending on the wrong level for most of the workforce. The strongest argument for using it is that it corrects the common assumption that pay is the whole story, and it does so in a form a manager can act on: it points at belonging, esteem and growth as rewards a business can supply. Its other weaknesses matter less in this setting than the diagnosis problem - the order is not fixed for everyone, and self-actualisation has no measure, but neither stops a manager acting sensibly. The practical course is to use the hierarchy to generate the options and then ask the employees, through consultation or a survey, which of them they would value, which is Vroom's valence test applied to a real workforce. The judgement would change in a small, uniform group whose circumstances the manager genuinely knows, where the diagnosis problem largely disappears.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether the manager of a 12-person workshop should use McClelland's theory to decide who does which work.
items.canonical_answer: She should use it, but as a hypothesis she tests rather than a classification she applies. The decisive criterion is the size of the workshop: with 12 employees she works alongside all of them and sees what each one does when given a choice, so the main weakness of the theory - that the dominant need is difficult to identify and the judgement is subjective - is far less damaging here than it would be across a workforce of hundreds. Acting on it costs her nothing but a reallocation of tasks, and the effect shows quickly in a small shop. The strongest argument against is that a misreading has consequences she cannot easily undo: an employee labelled as affiliation-driven and kept away from responsibility may be held back for years, and a dominant need can change as someone's circumstances change, so a judgement made once should not be treated as settled. items.prompt: Explain the difference between instrumentality and valence in Vroom's expectancy theory.
items.canonical_answer: Instrumentality is the employee's belief that reaching the required performance will actually bring the reward - will they pay it? items.prompt: A bonus scheme is rated by employees at expectancy 0.9, instrumentality 0.9 and valence 0.2. Explain what those three figures show about the scheme and what the business should change.

items.prompt: Analyse how introducing a motivation method without first diagnosing the unmet need can leave a business's costs where they were.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is a business that has identified a symptom - absence, turnover, poor quality - but not the need behind it. The mechanism is that a reward changes behaviour only where it answers a need that is currently pressing, so a method aimed at the wrong need is received as pleasant and ignored: employees take the social event or the small bonus and continue as before, because nothing they were short of has been supplied. items.prompt: A business paying its packers close to the national minimum wage is deciding between spending on job enrichment and spending the same amount on pay. Evaluate which it should do.
items.canonical_answer: It should correct pay first. The decisive criterion is which need is currently binding: at close to the national minimum, the wage is deciding whether a household covers its costs, so the need money answers is still pressing, and rewards that answer esteem or growth are being offered to people whose attention is elsewhere. Enriching a job in those circumstances is likely to produce very little, and it may be read as an attempt to extract more responsibility without more money, which would leave the business worse off than doing nothing. The strongest argument on the other side is a real one: pay increases are permanent, they raise the wage bill every year afterwards, and the returns to further increases fall once the wage is adequate, whereas enrichment builds the reward into the job and does not have to be bought again each period. That argument is right about the long run and wrong about the order. The sensible course is sequential - raise pay to a level the packers regard as adequate, then spend on enrichment, at which point it is likely to be the better-value option. The judgement would reverse in a business whose pay was already comfortably above what the local market requires, where further money would be reaching a need that is already largely met.

items.prompt: Analyse how a performance-related pay scheme that employees regard as unfairly assessed can reduce effort below what it was before the scheme.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is a scheme whose awards rest on a manager's judgement, and employees who believe that judgement follows favour rather than performance. The first mechanism is the one the scheme intended, reversed: an employee who believes the award does not follow performance has no reason to raise effort for it, so the incentive produces nothing. The second mechanism is the damaging one. The assessment has now told employees where they stand relative to colleagues, on a basis they reject, so the scheme has created a grievance that did not exist before, and a sense of unfair reward is itself a source of dissatisfaction on Herzberg's account. The measurable consequence is effort at or below its previous level, more disputes reaching managers, and resignations concentrated among employees who rated themselves highly and were placed low. For the business, the cost of the awards has been incurred and the output has not improved. The chain depends on the perception of unfairness rather than on the fact of it, which is why published criteria and evidence behind each assessment do most of the work in preventing it.

items.prompt: Analyse how a suggestion scheme can lower a manufacturer's costs.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is that employees on the line see things managers do not - a jig that has to be adjusted twice a shift, material scrapped because a template is wrong, a machine left running overnight. The scheme gives those observations a route to someone who can act, which they did not previously have. The mechanism is that each adopted proposal removes a recurring waste, and because the waste recurs, the saving repeats every period rather than once: a change that saves material on every batch keeps saving it. A payment for adopted suggestions strengthens the flow, because employees now have a reason to write proposals up rather than mention them and move on. The measurable consequence is a lower cost of output per unit, and for the business that widens the gap between price and cost. The chain depends on proposals actually being considered and answered: where employees submit suggestions and hear nothing, the flow stops within a few months and the scheme costs the administration without producing the savings.

items.prompt: A medium-sized Namibian manufacturer is considering putting two elected employee representatives on its board. Evaluate whether it should.
items.canonical_answer: It should not go straight to board representation; it should build the lower rungs first and reconsider in two or three years. The decisive criterion is whether the representatives would be able to contribute to the decisions a board actually takes - financing, capital spending, market strategy - and in a business with no history of consultation there is nothing on which employees would have built that understanding. Two representatives in that position are likely either to defer on everything, which makes the seat symbolic, or to oppose decisions they cannot yet weigh, which slows the board without improving it. The strongest argument the other way is real and should not be dismissed: a seat on the board is the only rung that gives employees a vote rather than a hearing, and a business that stops at consultation may find employees conclude the exercise is a formality, which damages trust more than never asking. The answer to that is to make the consultation genuine rather than to skip to the top of the ladder - a works council with a right to be consulted on stated matters, and management visibly acting on what comes back. The judgement would change if the manufacturer already ran effective consultation and its employees were familiar with its finances, in which case board representation would be the next rung rather than a leap.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the argument must rest on a medium-sized manufacturer with no established consultation.
Criterion: the decisive factor is whether representatives could contribute to the decisions a board takes.
Counterargument: must give the real case for board representation - a vote rather than a hearing - and the risk of token consultation.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement - established consultation and employees familiar with the finances.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of giving employees a share in the management and control of a business.
items.canonical_answer: Decisions take longer, because views have to be collected, discussed and answered before the matter can be settled. The developed consequence is that the cost falls unevenly: for a decision about how a department organises its work the delay costs little and the decision is usually better, but for a decision that has to be made this week - a supplier failing, a large order that has to be accepted or refused - the same process can mean the opportunity is gone before the consultation is finished. This is why businesses that consult widely usually reserve a class of urgent decisions from the arrangement.

items.prompt: A Namibian mine has run a monthly consultative committee for three years. Attendance has fallen from 40 employees to 6, and the same three proposals have been raised each year. Explain what has gone wrong and what the mine should do.
items.canonical_answer: The committee is being read as a formality, and the evidence is in the two facts given. Proposals raised in three successive years are proposals that have not been answered; falling attendance is what employees do once they conclude that saying something changes nothing. The mechanism is that being asked raises an expectation, and an expectation repeatedly disappointed leaves employees more sceptical than never having been asked at all - which is why the mine now has a committee that is worse than useless, because it is consuming management and employee time and teaching the workforce that its judgement is not valued. What the mine should do follows directly: take the three standing proposals, decide each one, and give the committee a reason and a date for each decision, including the ones refused. A refusal that is explained restores the link between saying something and something happening; silence is what broke it.

Reasoning: the mechanism is that unanswered proposals teach employees that consultation changes nothing.
Conclusion: a specific remedy must be reached, and it must cover refused proposals as well as accepted ones.

items.prompt: Kavango Tiles employs 45 production staff on a time rate of N$34 an hour for a 40-hour week. Output averages 9 000 tiles a week and the reject rate is 6%. The owner is considering two schemes. Scheme A pays a weekly team bonus of N$18 000, shared equally, in any week when output exceeds 10 000 tiles. Scheme B adds performance-related pay of up to 5% of basic pay, assessed each quarter against individual objectives that include output, rejects and attendance. Calculate the weekly basic pay of one employee and the bonus each would receive under Scheme A; calculate the maximum weekly value of Scheme B to one employee; and evaluate which scheme the owner should adopt.
items.canonical_answer:
Basic pay for one employee is 40 x N$34 = N$1 360 a week. Under Scheme A the bonus per employee is N$18 000 / 45 = N$400 in a qualifying week, which is 400 / 1 360 = 29.4% of basic pay for that week. Under Scheme B the maximum weekly value is N$1 360 x 0.05 = N$68, which is about a sixth of what Scheme A pays in a week it triggers.

Judgement: the owner should adopt Scheme B, and should not adopt Scheme A in the form proposed. The decisive criterion is what each scheme pays for. Scheme A pays for tiles produced and says nothing about the 6% reject rate, so it rewards exactly the hurrying that produces rejects; at 9 000 tiles a week the plant already scraps 540 tiles, and a scheme pushing output to 10 000 without a quality condition is likely to raise that number. Scheme B assesses output, rejects and attendance together, so an employee cannot gain by trading one against another.

The strongest argument for Scheme A is its size. N$400 in a qualifying week against a maximum of N$68 is a difference employees can feel, and a scheme worth 5% of pay assessed quarterly may be too small to change behaviour at all - a real risk with performance pay. The owner should answer that by widening Scheme B's range rather than by returning to Scheme A, because the fault in A is what it measures and no increase in the amount corrects that. Scheme A also requires no assessment, while Scheme B needs a supervisor's time for 45 quarterly reviews and will fail if staff regard the ratings as arbitrary.

The condition on the recommendation is therefore the assessment: Scheme B is the better scheme provided Kavango Tiles publishes its criteria in advance and shows each employee the evidence behind their rating. If it cannot resource that, the better course is Scheme A amended - a bonus that triggers on 10 000 tiles only in a week when rejects stay at or below 6% - which keeps the size of the incentive and removes the distortion. The figure to watch is the reject rate, read weekly, whichever scheme is chosen.
marking_guidance: All four figures must be calculated with working shown: basic pay, the Scheme A bonus per employee, its percentage of basic pay, and the Scheme B maximum.
Judgement: the answer must recommend one scheme, not present both and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Kavango Tiles' own facts - the 6% reject rate and the 9 000-tile average.
Criterion: the decisive factor is what each scheme measures, not how much it pays.
Counterargument: must address the size difference between N$400 and N$68 and the risk that a small award changes nothing.
Condition: must state what the recommendation depends on - a resourced and transparent assessment - and what to do if it is absent.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Etosha Fresh, a vegetable packing business employing 120 seasonal and 30 permanent staff, has a 34% annual labour turnover among its permanent staff and pays them 8% below the going rate in the district. Evaluate whether it should raise pay or introduce non-financial motivators to reduce that turnover.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: correct the 8% pay gap first, then spend on non-financial methods; the two are sequential rather than alternatives.

Paragraph 1 - what the evidence actually says. The two facts given point the same way: 34% turnover among permanent staff alongside pay 8% below the district rate is the pattern you would expect if employees can obtain a better wage nearby, and it identifies pay as the binding constraint. State this as the diagnosis the rest of the answer tests.

Paragraph 2 - the mechanism if pay is corrected. Closing the gap removes the reason for the comparison employees are currently making, so departures to local competitors fall; the business then avoids repeated recruitment spending, repeated induction, and the output lost while replacements learn. Note that on Herzberg's account this removes dissatisfaction rather than creating effort, which is precisely why it is a first step and not the whole answer.

Paragraph 3 - the strongest case for non-financial methods instead. They cost less in cash, which matters to a seasonal business with uneven revenue; a permanent increase raises the wage bill every year afterwards; and once pay is adequate, further money does progressively less. Concede that this argument is correct about the long run.

Paragraph 4 - why it does not win here. Non-financial methods are not free - training fees, lost output, management time - and offered while pay sits 8% below the district rate they answer a need that is not the one pressing, and may be read as a way of avoiding the increase. The seasonal workforce is a separate question: for staff employed for a few weeks, the methods that depend on a long relationship, such as development and promotion, have little to work on.

Judgement and condition: close the gap, then spend on responsibility, recognition and development for the 30 permanent staff, and watch the turnover figure for that group. The judgement would change if turnover persisted after the gap was closed, because that would identify a need money was not answering.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay - structure with a stated judgement is what is assessed.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached.
Context: the plan must use Etosha Fresh's own facts - the 34% turnover, the 8% pay gap and the seasonal workforce.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be which need is currently binding, evidenced by the pay gap.
Counterargument: must include the genuine case for non-financial methods, and concede what is right about it.
Condition: must end on what would change the answer - turnover persisting after the gap is closed.

items.prompt: Namib Coast Cannery employs 380 people. Head office sets shift patterns, and supervisors refer every change to a production manager. Absence runs at 12%, three lines have missed their output target for six consecutive months, and an internal survey found that 71% of staff said nobody asks their opinion. The board has budgeted N$600 000 for a response. Analyse the circumstances under which employee participation would improve the cannery's performance, and evaluate what it should do with the budget.
items.canonical_answer:
The circumstances are present here in an unusually clear form. Participation improves performance where the people doing the work hold information the decision-makers do not, where the decisions in question are ones employees know something about, and where management will act on what comes back. All three conditions fit: shift patterns are set at head office by people who do not work them, 71% of staff report that nobody asks, and absence at 12% alongside six months of missed targets is exactly the pattern that unworkable rosters and unreported line problems produce.

It would not improve performance where employees lack the information to judge the question - the cannery's pricing, its capital spending, its choice of markets are not matters a line team can weigh - and where management consults and then changes nothing, which would leave the workforce more sceptical than the survey already shows.

Recommendation: spend the budget on two rungs of the ladder rather than one grand arrangement. First, a joint consultative committee with elected representatives from each line, meeting monthly, with a written answer and a date required for every proposal - including the refusals. Second, and this is where the larger part of the money should go, empower each line team to set its own shift roster within stated limits and to stop the line on a quality fault, which requires training and the production information the teams do not currently see. The decisive factor is that the cannery's problem is not a shortage of goodwill but a structure in which the people closest to the work have no authority and no route for what they know; consultation supplies the route and empowerment supplies the authority.

The strongest argument against is speed: decisions now taken by one production manager will take longer once teams are involved, and a cannery handling perishable input cannot afford delay at every point. That is why the empowerment should be bounded - stated limits on rostering, an explicit reserved class of urgent decisions - rather than open. The recommendation is conditional on the production manager accepting the decisions that come back; if reversals become routine, the arrangement will be read as the survey already reads head office, and the N$600 000 will have bought a more articulate form of the same problem. The figures to read after twelve months are the absence rate and the three lines' output against target.
marking_guidance: Both the circumstances favouring participation and those against it must be analysed before recommending.
Judgement: a recommendation for the budget is required.
Context: must use the cannery's own facts - the 12% absence, six months of missed targets, the 71% survey figure and head-office rostering.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be that the people closest to the work have neither authority nor a route for what they know.
Counterargument: must address the loss of speed in a business handling perishable input.
Condition: must state what would undermine the recommendation - managers reversing the decisions that come back.

items.prompt: A manager has been told that morale in her department is poor. Identify the questions she should ask before choosing a way to respond, and explain what each one would tell her.
items.canonical_answer:
What do the figures say, and over what period? State the problem as days lost to absence, resignations, output per shift and reject rates before anything else, because 'morale is poor' does not indicate which need is unmet and each of those figures points somewhere different.

Is the pay in this department adequate for what the area costs, and how does it compare with what comparable employers pay? A wage below what a household needs means the binding constraint is physiological or security, and rewards aimed above that level will do little.

How secure is the work? Short contracts, uncertain hours or an announced restructuring leave the security need unmet, and the behaviour that follows is people looking elsewhere rather than people working less.

Do these employees work alone or alongside others? Isolated work leaves the need to belong unmet, and the remedy is in how the work is organised rather than in what it pays.

Is anyone's work noticed, and is there anywhere to progress to? Work whose results go unnoticed and a job with no route out of it leave the needs for respect and for growth unmet, which is the pattern among long-serving staff whose pay is already settled.

Are the answers the same for everyone in the department? They usually are not: each employee arrives with different circumstances, and a single response offered to all of them will reach some and pass others by.

And which figure will show whether the response worked, and by when? Naming it in advance is what converts a failed attempt into a corrected diagnosis rather than a closed question.
marking_guidance: State each question plainly before explaining it.
Give the reason each question matters - what the answer would tell the manager about which need is unmet.
Use the context: these are questions about one department, and the answer must recognise that employees in it may differ.
The answer must include the measure to be read afterwards, because a response without one cannot be judged.

items.prompt: Otjiwarongo Crates makes wooden crates. It currently pays its 12 assemblers a time rate of N$30 an hour for a 40-hour week, and each assembler completes an average of 96 crates a week. The owner is considering a piece rate of N$13.50 a crate with a guaranteed weekly minimum of N$1 100. She expects output per assembler to rise to 110 crates a week. Rejected crates, currently 3% of output, are scrapped at a materials cost of N$46 each. Calculate the weekly pay of an average assembler under each method and the weekly wage cost for all 12; calculate the scrap cost at the current reject rate; and evaluate whether she should change to the piece rate.
items.canonical_answer:
Under the time rate, weekly pay is 40 x N$30 = N$1 200 an assembler, so the wage cost for twelve is 12 x N$1 200 = N$14 400 a week, and weekly output is 12 x 96 = 1 152 crates.

Under the piece rate at the expected 110 crates, pay is 110 x N$13.50 = N$1 485 an assembler, above the guaranteed minimum, so the wage cost for twelve is 12 x N$1 485 = N$17 820 a week and output is 12 x 110 = 1 320 crates.

Labour cost per crate falls from N$14 400 / 1 152 = N$12.50 to N$17 820 / 1 320 = N$13.50. Scrap at the current 3% is 1 152 x 0.03 = 34.56 crates a week, costing 34.56 x N$46 = N$1 589.76.

Judgement: she should not change to the piece rate as it stands. The decisive criterion is that labour cost per crate rises rather than falls - from N$12.50 to N$13.50, because the rate of N$13.50 a crate is above what an assembler currently costs per crate at the time rate. The extra 168 crates a week are therefore being bought at a rate higher than the business currently pays, which only makes sense if those crates can be sold and if the margin on them exceeds the difference.

The reject rate makes the case worse. Paying for crates completed pays nothing for crates completed well, so the 3% is likely to rise; at the higher output, each percentage point of rejects costs 1 320 x 0.01 = 13.2 crates, or 13.2 x N$46 = N$607.20 a week in materials alone, before any labour is counted.

The strongest argument for the change is real: output per assembler rises by 14 crates, which matters a great deal if the business is turning orders away, and a piece rate makes the labour cost per crate predictable, which a time rate does not. The answer to it is to set the rate below the current labour cost per crate rather than above it - at N$12.00 a crate the twelve assemblers would cost 12 x N$1 320 = N$15 840 for 1 320 crates, a labour cost of N$12.00 a crate - and to make the rate conditional on the assembler's own reject rate. The recommendation is therefore conditional on two things she must establish first: that the extra output can be sold, and that rejects can be attributed to the assembler who made them.
marking_guidance: All the figures must be calculated with working shown: weekly pay under each method, the wage cost for twelve, output, labour cost per crate and the scrap cost.
Judgement: the answer must recommend, not present both cases and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Otjiwarongo Crates' own figures, in particular its current labour cost per crate.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that the proposed rate is above the current labour cost per crate.
Counterargument: must address the genuine gain in output per assembler and the predictability of the labour cost.
Condition: must name what the recommendation depends on - the extra output being saleable, and rejects being attributable.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Windhoek Precision employs 60 machinists. It pays 12% above the district going rate, offers permanent contracts and medical aid, and has just refurbished its canteen. Output per machinist has not moved in three years and two of its four most experienced machinists resigned last year, saying the work had become dull. Evaluate what the company should do to raise output per machinist.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: change the content of the jobs rather than the conditions around them - give machining teams responsibility for complete components including set-up and quality checks - because the evidence shows the hygiene factors are already settled.

Paragraph 1 - what the facts establish. Pay 12% above the district rate, permanent contracts, medical aid and a refurbished canteen mean the physiological and safety levels of Maslow's hierarchy are largely met for these employees, and Herzberg's hygiene factors have been attended to. The resignations were not about pay, because the two machinists gave a different reason. Establish that the diagnosis is not money.

Paragraph 2 - why more of the same will not work. A satisfied need loses its power to direct behaviour, and correcting a hygiene factor removes dissatisfaction without creating effort. Another increase, or another improvement to the surroundings, is spending on a scale that is already at neutral - which is exactly the pattern of three flat years alongside rising conditions.

Paragraph 3 - the mechanism of the proposed change. Enrichment gives a complete and identifiable unit of work, the authority to decide how it is done and direct feedback on the result. For machinists that means owning a component from set-up to inspection: achievement becomes visible, responsibility is real, and the people best placed to correct a drifting process are the ones who see it first. Reach output per machinist and the reject rate as the measures.

Paragraph 4 - the strongest arguments against. Enrichment takes authority from setters and inspectors, who may resist it; it needs training and output may dip while it is learned; and machinists carrying inspection responsibility may reasonably ask to be regraded, so the change should not be costed as free. Herzberg's evidence also came from professional employees, so its transfer to a machining floor is an assumption rather than a finding - which is a reason to pilot the change on one cell and read the figures.

Judgement and condition: pilot enrichment on one cell, with training and a regrading position settled in advance, and read output per machinist and the reject rate after six months. The judgement would change if the pilot showed output constrained by the machines rather than by the machinists, because motivation is one determinant of productivity among several and the binding one here would then be capital, not effort.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay - structure with a stated judgement is what is assessed.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached.
Context: the plan must use Windhoek Precision's own facts - the 12% pay premium, the canteen, three flat years and the stated reason for the resignations.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be that the hygiene factors are already settled, so further spending on them acts where the need is met.
Counterargument: must include resistance from setters and inspectors, the output dip, the likely regrading claim and the professional sample Herzberg drew on.
Condition: must end on what would change the answer - output constrained by the machines rather than by the machinists.

items.prompt: A guest lodge has three problems: kitchen staff complain about broken equipment, experienced guides say the work has become routine, and a new punctuality bonus is being ignored. Explain which theory is the right tool for each problem.
items.canonical_answer: Each problem sits at a different point, so a single theory would answer one of them and miss two. The broken kitchen equipment is a hygiene factor in Herzberg's sense: it surrounds the work, it is causing dissatisfaction, and repairing it removes a complaint rather than creating enthusiasm - but it still has to be done, because the complaint is real. The guides' problem is different in kind. Experienced staff saying the work has become routine are describing an unmet need to grow, which is the top of Maslow's hierarchy, and the answer is a larger role, a specialist route or training rather than anything done to the surroundings. The ignored bonus is neither: it is a question about whether a reward on offer will be chased, which is what Vroom's process theory answers, so the lodge should test whether the target is reachable, whether staff believe the payment will follow, and whether they value it. The conclusion the lodge should draw is that the three problems need three different responses, and that diagnosing which is which comes before choosing any of them.

Reasoning: the mechanism is that content theories answer what is unmet while a process theory answers whether a reward will be chased.

items.prompt: A brick works moulds, stacks and loads by hand. Output per worker varies from 260 to 520 bricks a shift and no two workers use the same method. The manager has read Taylor. Explain what Taylor's approach would have him do here, and what it would put at risk.
items.canonical_answer: Taylor's approach fits the observable facts closely. With output varying by a factor of two and no two workers using the same method, he would have the manager time the job, break it into its elements, identify the quickest sound way to perform each, set a standard output from the timings, train every worker to that one method, and pay a piece rate above the standard. The reason the approach applies here at all is that bricks are countable and attributable, which is the condition the whole method assumes and which much service work fails. What it puts at risk is what the count does not capture. A rate per brick pays nothing for a brick moulded well, so the works would need to add inspection, and hand-loading under time pressure raises the chance of injury - a cost the output figure does not show. The manager should therefore adopt the method study and the standard, and pay on a measure that includes rejects rather than on bricks alone.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the works' own facts - the 260 to 520 range, the absence of a common method, and hand loading.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that countable attributable output is the condition Taylor's method assumes.
Conclusion: a recommendation must be reached that keeps the method study and modifies the pay measure.

items.prompt: A canning factory moved its line workers from benches facing each other into individual booths to reduce talking. Output fell 8% over the following quarter and two experienced workers resigned. Explain what Mayo's work suggests happened.
items.canonical_answer: The factory removed something it had not counted as part of the work. On Mayo's account the group a person works in influences what they are willing to give: belonging to it, being known by the others and having the company of colleagues are received at work, and the benches facing each other were what supplied them. Moving workers into individual booths removed the group without changing anything else, and output fell 8%. The mechanism runs through motivation rather than through the mechanics of canning - nobody's hands are slower in a booth - and the two resignations point the same way, since experienced workers with options are the ones who leave when a job becomes less bearable. The conclusion for the factory is that the talking it was trying to eliminate was doing work it had not attributed to it, and that if the booths stay it has to supply belonging some other way, through team tasks, shared breaks or a group responsible for a whole batch.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the factory's own facts - benches replaced by booths, the 8% fall and the two resignations.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the group supplies belonging, which influences what workers give.
Conclusion: the answer must reach what the factory should do if the booths remain.

items.prompt: A pharmacy chain pays its dispensing staff a time rate and its front-shop staff a small basic wage plus 5% commission on over-the-counter sales. A pharmacy inspector has queried whether the second arrangement is appropriate. Explain why the chain pays the two groups differently and why the inspector may have a point.
items.canonical_answer: The chain has matched the tightness of the pay link to what it wants more of in each role. Dispensing is work in which an error is dangerous and speed is not the objective, so a time rate is used: it pays for hours and gives the dispenser no financial reason to hurry. Front-shop selling is countable and attributable, so commission ties part of the pay to the measured result and supplies an incentive the time rate does not. The inspector's point follows from the same logic applied to the front shop. Commission pays on the value sold rather than on whether the product suited the customer, and in a pharmacy the customer is often buying a remedy on advice, so the arrangement gives staff a reason to recommend towards the higher-value product. The chain should conclude that the tighter link is right for the front shop only if the measure is changed - commission on a basket that excludes advice-led products, or a cap - because the distortion here reaches a customer's health and not only the chain's repeat trade.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the chain's own facts - a time rate for dispensing, 5% commission in the front shop, and the inspector's query.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the tightness of the pay link decides what receives attention and what does not.
Conclusion: the answer must reach why the inspector may be right and what the chain should change.

items.prompt: A bus company's drivers are paid 14% above the regional average and have permanent contracts. Absence is low, but drivers take no interest in the vehicle-condition reports the company depends on, and the depot manager says they do the job and nothing more. Explain why non-financial methods are the right instrument here.
items.canonical_answer: Because the facts show that pay has already done what pay can do. Drivers on 14% above the regional average with permanent contracts have their physiological and security needs answered, and the low absence figure confirms that the arrangement is not causing dissatisfaction - in Herzberg's terms the hygiene factors are settled. That is exactly the position in which further money reaches a need that is already met, so a third route has to be found for the behaviour the company actually wants. 'They do the job and nothing more' is a description of work that contains no achievement, no responsibility and no feedback, and the vehicle-condition reports are the obvious place to change that: give each driver the authority to take a vehicle off the road, report each driver's own defect record back to them, and let experienced drivers train new ones. The company should not treat this as the cheap option - it costs training time and some disruption when a vehicle is withdrawn - but it is the instrument that fits the diagnosis.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the company's own facts - pay 14% above the regional average, permanent contracts, low absence and the neglected reports.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that money reaches a need already met, so the remaining rewards are the non-financial ones.
Conclusion: the answer must reach specific measures and must not present them as free.

context.situation: well-paid drivers doing the minimum
facts: drivers paid 14% above the regional average
